There is genuine disagreement among sources on whether a degree is necessary to become a successful graphic designer. Some sources argue that a degree is essential: [d1] states that "for most entry-level and advanced graphic design positions, you will need a minimum of a bachelor's degree from an accredited university, college, or private design school," and [d6] notes that "most employers are looking for designers with a more complete and well-rounded education – the kind only a college degree can provide," citing the U.S. Department of Labor's finding that a bachelor's degree greatly improves job prospects. On the other hand, [d2] directly states that a degree "is not a requirement" and that "many companies hire entry level designers based solely on their portfolio and experience," while [d4] flatly answers "No, a degree is not required to become a graphic designer," pointing out that most companies focus on portfolio and work experience and that most graphic design jobs worldwide do not require a degree. [d3] and [d8] similarly note that many successful designers are self-taught and never completed a formal degree programme. A middle-ground view is offered by [d9], which summarizes: "A degree is not a requirement, but it helps," and by [d5] and [d10], which acknowledge that while formal education is beneficial and employers value knowledge and skills, it is not strictly necessary to hold a degree to succeed in the field.
